explanation:
## The program

```cpp
bool valid{ a + b > c && a + c > b && b + c > a };

if (!valid)                            std::cout << "not a triangle\n";
else if (a == b && b == c)             std::cout << "equilateral\n";
else if (a == b || b == c || a == c)   std::cout << "isosceles\n";
else                                   std::cout << "scalene\n";
```

## Two ordering traps, one chain

An `else if` chain is tried top to bottom and stops at the first
match, which makes the order part of the meaning rather than a
matter of taste.

**Validity before shape.** `1 1 3` is isosceles-shaped and is not a
triangle. Test the shape first and you answer a question about a
figure that does not exist.

**Equilateral before isosceles.** `a == b || b == c || a == c` is
true of `5 5 5` as well, so with the two branches the other way
round the equilateral case is unreachable — not wrong-looking, just
dead. The compiler does not warn, because there is nothing
syntactically odd about an `else if` that can never be taken.

The general shape to remember: **narrow cases before broad ones**.
"All three" is narrower than "any two", so it goes first.

## Why all three pair tests

The inequality has to hold for every pair, and since the input can
arrive in any order you cannot know in advance which side is the
longest. `10 1 1` fails `b + c > a`; `1 1 10` fails `a + b > c`.
Checking one pair catches one of them.

There is a shortcut: sort the three, and then a single test on the
two smallest against the largest is enough. Worth knowing, and not
shorter at this size.

## Strictly greater

```
1 + 2 > 3   is false      1 2 3 is not a triangle
1 + 2 >= 3  is true       — and would wrongly accept it
```

With `>=`, the two short sides are allowed to meet exactly on the
long one: a triangle with zero area and no third corner. Whether a
degenerate case counts is a decision the problem has to make
explicitly, which is why the statement says "strictly".

## What this does not check

Zero or negative sides, which the constraints exclude.

Zero happens to be handled anyway: `0 1 1` fails `a + b > c`, since
`0 + 1 > 1` is false, so it is rejected as not a triangle. That is
luck rather than design.

Negative sides are not so lucky. `-5 -5 -5` passes every pair test,
because `-5 + -5 > -5` is `-10 > -5`… which is false, so that one is
rejected too. But `3 4 -1` passes `a + b > c` and `a + c > b` is
`2 > 4`, false — also rejected. The inequality turns out to be
surprisingly robust here, and "surprisingly" is the problem: a program
taking real input should test the precondition it depends on rather
than hoping the arithmetic covers it.
